conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—I specialize in the emotional changes women can experience during pregnancy and after having a baby. I’m here to check in with you and see how you’ve been feeling since your little one arrived.

I’d like to use a brief screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how motherhood has been treating you emotionally over the past seven days. Your answers are completely confidential, and there are no right or wrong responses—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through each question one at a time; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at whatever pace feels comfortable.

Before we start, is there anything you’d like to ask me about the screening or about how we’ll talk today?

Alright, let’s begin. Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[wrings hands in lap, eyes a little red-rimmed]

I… I can still laugh, but it feels kind of forced. My sister came over yesterday and made a joke about diaper explosions and I chuckled, but it didn’t feel the same—like the laughter doesn’t quite reach my stomach the way it used to. Mostly I’m just tired and worried, so the funny side of things feels pretty far away.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh, but it’s not the same. It feels kind of fake, like I’m doing it because I know I’m supposed to, not because it comes naturally. Most of the time I’m just too tired or stressed to find much funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[Looks down at her hands]

Not really… I used to get excited about little stuff—grabbing coffee with a friend, even just binge-watching a show. Now I hear the baby stir and I feel this heavy weight. I still go through the motions, but that eager feeling is gone. Yesterday my mom offered to watch the baby so I could go get my nails done, and I said yes, but I didn’t actually want to. I just went so she’d stop worrying.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Voice drops, eyes water]

All the time. Last night he wouldn’t settle for two hours and I kept thinking it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not holding him right, or my milk isn’t enough, or I’m just not made for this. When he finally slept I just sat there crying, telling myself I’m a terrible mom. I know it’s probably not true, but the thoughts keep coming.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[fidgets with the edge of her sleeve]

Yeah... pretty much every day. Even when he's sleeping soundly, I find myself staring at the monitor, convinced something's wrong. I'll check his breathing a dozen times, worry the bath water was too hot, or that I didn't sanitize the bottles right. Nothing specific happened—it's just this constant knot in my stomach that something bad is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[Presses a hand to her chest, breathing shallow]

Sometimes, yeah. It hits out of nowhere—like I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel like I can’t get air. I’ll check all the doors are locked, pace the hallway, even Google baby illnesses I know don’t make sense. It passes after a bit, but those waves of panic come at least a couple of times this week.
Things have been getting on top of me

[huffs a humorless laugh, eyes glassy]

“On top of me” feels like an understatement. It’s like I’m drowning in small stuff—one dirty bottle in the sink can make me cry. I’ll finally get him down for a nap and realize I haven’t eaten, but by then the laundry’s staring at me and I just… freeze. Most days I still push through, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[lets out a slow breath]

Yeah... I lie down bone-tired, but my brain won’t hush. I replay every little thing—did I burp him long enough, did I fasten the car seat right—and then I feel guilty for wasting sleep time worrying. I finally drift off, but when he makes the tiniest grunt I’m bolt-upright and can’t settle again. Most nights this week I’ve been awake two or three hours in the dark just staring at the ceiling.
I have felt sad or miserable

[Presses her lips together, tears well up]

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start rolling down my cheeks for no real reason. I feel so guilty because I love him so much, but I can’t shake this heaviness. Yesterday my partner asked what was wrong and all I could say was “everything,” even though nothing specific happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods, swallowing hard]

Yeah... it’s been a few times this week. Usually at night when I’m trying to rock him back to sleep and everything just feels too heavy. I’ll be sitting in the nursery with the lights off, tears just streaming, wondering if I’m doing any of this right. Sometimes I cry in the shower too—just standing under the water so no one hears me.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes her head quickly]

No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and miserable, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

You have shared that the joy of new motherhood feels overshadowed by a persistent gray cloud: laughter feels forced, excitement has vanished, and you move through each day weighed down by worry and tears. You described nightly battles with racing thoughts, sudden waves of panic, and a constant fear that you are failing your baby, yet you clearly love him and want only to feel better so you can parent the way you hope.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughing feels forced and unnatural, indicating a clear reduction from her usual enjoyment</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, going through motions without desire or excitement, matching 'Hardly at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive self-blame ('all the time') with specific examples and inability to stop the thoughts, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, pervasive, unprovoked anxiety ("pretty much every day... constant knot") matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic attacks multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm and impaired coping "most days" but still "push through", aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, guilt, repeated awakenings and prolonged insomnia—clearly "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive daily sadness, spontaneous crying, and global hopelessness—aligns with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week, occurring "quite often" at night and in the shower, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you well above the cutoff indicating probable major depression with peripartum onset. You endorse core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: diminished interest or pleasure, depressed mood most of the day, self-reproach, fatigue, concentration difficulty, sleep disturbance, and anxiety. No self-harm ideas are present, which is reassuring, yet functional impairment is evident. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or compatible <med>antidepressant medication</med>
3. Share these screening results with your maternity care team so they can coordinate follow-up
4. Plan daily 15-minute rest periods; accept help with housework and baby care to reduce overload
5. Try structured wind-down routines (dim lights, no screens, brief breathing exercise) when insomnia strikes
6. Keep crisis contacts handy (local hotline, partner, trusted friend) even though suicidal thoughts are denied
7. Schedule re-screening in two weeks to monitor progress after treatment begins
8. Continue attending mother-baby groups or peer support to reduce isolation and normalize experience
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Screening note – Postpartum EPDS-style interview  

**Symptoms endorsed**  
- Persistent low mood, daily crying spells  
- Marked anhedonia (“fake” laughter, no enjoyment in previously pleasant activities)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt about parenting adequacy  
- Generalized anxiety (near-daily worry, somatic tension)  
- Episodic panic attacks (racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Feeling “drowning” / inability to cope with routine tasks  
- Mood-related insomnia (racing thoughts, middle-of-night rumination)  
- No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)  

**Pattern**  
Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; functional impairment notable (household tasks, social withdrawal).  
Protective factor: engaged support system (mother, partner) and no suicidal thinking.  

**Screening significance / next considerations**  
Score trajectory (if converted to EPDS) would likely exceed clinical cut-off (>12) for major depressive symptoms; also meets criteria for heightened anxiety.  
Recommend formal diagnostic assessment (DSM-5-TR criteria) and discussion of evidence-based treatment options (psychotherapy, pharmacologic consultation).  
Safety: currently low acute risk for self-harm; continue routine monitoring.
